A GeoJSON of neighborhood boundaries (city open-data portals almost always have one) drives both the dropdown and the map, so names always match. ``` lanternfly/ ├── app.py ├── build_site.py ├── neighborhoods.geojson ├── requirements.txt ├── data/ (auto-created: DB + photos, keep OUT of web root) └── public/ (generated: leaderboard.html, map.html; serve this) ``` **requirements.txt** ``` flask>=3.0 flask-limiter>=3.5 pillow>=10.0 folium>=0.15 branca>=0.7 gunicorn>=21.0 ``` ### app.py ```python """Stomp the Lanternfly: submission form.""" import hashlib import json import os import sqlite3 import uuid from datetime import datetime, timezone from pathlib import Path from flask import Flask, abort, g, render_template_string, request from flask_limiter import Limiter from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address from PIL import Image, ImageOps from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix BASE = Path(__file__).parent DATA_DIR = BASE / "data" DB_PATH = DATA_DIR / "lanternfly.db" PHOTO_DIR = DATA_DIR / "photos" GEOJSON_PATH = BASE / "neighborhoods.geojson" NAME_FIELD = os.environ.get("NEIGHBORHOOD_FIELD", "name") IP_SALT = os.environ.get("IP_SALT", "change-me") ID_GUIDE_URL = os.environ.get("ID_GUIDE_URL", "#") # extension ID page STATE_REPORT_URL = os.environ.get("STATE_REPORT_URL", "") # state ag sighting form MAX_KILLS = 10_000 # hard reject above this KILL_REVIEW = 1_000 # held as 'pending' at or above this MAX_EGG_MASSES = 2_000 EGG_REVIEW = 200 Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = 40_000_000 # decompression-bomb guard # Methods for adults/nymphs. METHODS = { "stomp": "Stomped / swatted", "circle_trap": "Circle trap", "guarded_band": "Sticky band with wire-mesh wildlife guard", "vacuum": "Vacuum / net", "other": "Other", "none": "None, only reporting egg masses", } with open(GEOJSON_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f: NEIGHBORHOODS = sorted( feat["properties"][NAME_FIELD] for feat in json.load(f)["features"] ) NEIGHBORHOOD_SET = set(NEIGHBORHOODS) app = Flask(__name__) app.config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 12 * 1024 * 1024 app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_for=1) # real client IP behind nginx limiter = Limiter( get_remote_address, app=app, storage_uri=os.environ.get("RATELIMIT_STORAGE", "memory://"), ) SCHEMA = """ CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS submissions ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, created_at TEXT NOT NULL, neighborhood TEXT NOT NULL, kills INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, egg_masses INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, method TEXT NOT NULL, photo TEXT, photo_ok INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'approved', ip_hash TEXT ); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_status_hood ON submissions(status, neighborhood); """ def init_db(): DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) PHOTO_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn: conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL") conn.executescript(SCHEMA) def get_db(): if "db" not in g: g.db = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, timeout=10) g.db.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout=10000") return g.db @app.teardown_appcontext def close_db(_exc): db = g.pop("db", None) if db is not None: db.close() def save_photo(fileobj) -> str: """Re-encode as JPEG; this drops EXIF/GPS metadata entirely.""" try: img = Image.open(fileobj.stream) img = ImageOps.exif_transpose(img) # keep orientation before stripping img = img.convert("RGB") img.thumbnail((1600, 1600)) except Exception: abort(400, "We couldn't read that photo. Please try a JPEG or PNG.") name = f"{uuid.uuid4().hex}.jpg" img.save(PHOTO_DIR / name, "JPEG", quality=85) # no exif= arg, so none saved return name def parse_count(field: str, upper: int) -> int: raw = request.form.get(field, "").strip() or "0" try: n = int(raw) except ValueError: abort(400, "Please enter whole numbers.") if not 0 <= n <= upper: abort(400, f"Counts must be between 0 and {upper:,}.") return n FORM_HTML = """ Stomp the Lanternfly: Report Your Count

Report your lanternfly count

Sure it's a spotted lanternfly? Some native moths and leafhoppers look similar, especially the nymphs. Check the ID guide.
Using a sticky band? Cage it in wire mesh so birds, bats and frogs can't get stuck. Circle traps work without exposed glue. Check traps and bands often and release anything that isn't a lanternfly. If an animal does get stuck, don't pull it free; contact a wildlife rehabilitator. Each mass holds about 30–50 eggs, so this is one of the biggest things you can do.
""" THANKS_HTML = """ Thanks!

Thanks, your count is in!

The leaderboard updates every few minutes.

{% if state_url %}

Seeing lanternflies somewhere new? Please also report the sighting to the state. It helps track the spread.

{% endif %}

Report another

""" @app.get("/") def form(): return render_template_string( FORM_HTML, neighborhoods=NEIGHBORHOODS, methods=METHODS, max_kills=MAX_KILLS, max_eggs=MAX_EGG_MASSES, id_url=ID_GUIDE_URL, ) @app.post("/submit") @limiter.limit("10 per hour") def submit(): if request.form.get("website"): # honeypot: bots fill it, humans don't return render_template_string(THANKS_HTML, state_url=STATE_REPORT_URL) hood = request.form.get("neighborhood", "") if hood not in NEIGHBORHOOD_SET: abort(400, "Please choose a neighborhood from the list.") kills = parse_count("kills", MAX_KILLS) eggs = parse_count("egg_masses", MAX_EGG_MASSES) if kills + eggs == 0: abort(400, "Please enter at least one lanternfly or egg mass.") method = request.form.get("method", "") if method not in METHODS: abort(400, "Please choose a method from the list.") if kills > 0 and method == "none": abort(400, "Please tell us how you got the adults/nymphs.") photo = None upload = request.files.get("photo") if upload and upload.filename: photo = save_photo(upload) status = "pending" if (kills >= KILL_REVIEW or eggs >= EGG_REVIEW) else "approved" ip = request.remote_addr or "" db = get_db() db.execute( "INSERT INTO submissions (created_at, neighborhood, kills, egg_masses, method," " photo, photo_ok, status, ip_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", ( datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"), hood, kills, eggs, method, photo, 1 if request.form.get("photo_ok") else 0, status, hashlib.sha256((IP_SALT + ip).encode()).hexdigest()[:16], ), ) db.commit() return render_template_string(THANKS_HTML, state_url=STATE_REPORT_URL) init_db() ``` ### build_site.py ```python """Generate static leaderboard and map from approved submissions.""" import html import json import os import sqlite3 import tempfile from datetime import datetime from pathlib import Path import branca.colormap as cm import folium BASE = Path(__file__).parent DB_PATH = BASE / "data" / "lanternfly.db" GEOJSON_PATH = BASE / "neighborhoods.geojson" OUT_DIR = BASE / "public" NAME_FIELD = os.environ.get("NEIGHBORHOOD_FIELD", "name") # ties share a rank rank, prev = i, s[RANK_BY] rows.append( f"{rank}{html.escape(name)}" f"{s['kills']:,}{s['egg_masses']:,}" f"{s['impact']:,}{s['reports']:,}" ) total_k = sum(s["kills"] for s in stats.values()) total_e = sum(s["egg_masses"] for s in stats.values()) return f""" Stomp the Lanternfly Leaderboard

Stomp the Lanternfly Leaderboard

{total_k:,} lanternflies and {total_e:,} egg masses reported. Updated {updated}.

Ranked by {LABELS.get(RANK_BY, RANK_BY).lower()}. Impact counts each egg mass as {EGGS_PER_MASS} lanternflies that never hatch.

{''.join(rows)}
#NeighborhoodKilledEgg masses ImpactReports

See the map

""" def build_map(geo, stats): vmax = max((s[RANK_BY] for s in stats.values()), default=0) or 1 cmap = cm.linear.YlOrRd_09.scale(0, vmax) cmap.caption = LABELS.get(RANK_BY, RANK_BY) empty = {"kills": 0, "egg_masses": 0, "reports": 0, "impact": 0, "average": 0} for feat in geo["features"]: s = stats.get(feat["properties"][NAME_FIELD], empty) for k in ("kills", "egg_masses", "reports"): feat["properties"][f"_{k}"] = s[k] feat["properties"]["_metric"] = s[RANK_BY] def style(feat): v = feat["properties"]["_metric"] return {"fillColor": cmap(v) if v else "#eeeeee", "color": "#555", "weight": 1, "fillOpacity": 0.7} m = folium.Map(tiles="cartodbpositron") layer = folium.GeoJson( geo, style_function=style, tooltip=folium.GeoJsonTooltip( fields=[NAME_FIELD, "_kills", "_egg_masses", "_reports"], aliases=["Neighborhood", "Killed", "Egg masses", "Reports"], localize=True), ) layer.add_to(m) cmap.add_to(m) m.fit_bounds(layer.get_bounds()) return m.get_root().render() def main(): OUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) with open(GEOJSON_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f: geo = json.load(f) names = [feat["properties"][NAME_FIELD] for feat in geo["features"]] stats = tally(names) updated = datetime.now().strftime("%b %d, %Y at %I:%M %p") atomic_write(OUT_DIR / "leaderboard.html", build_leaderboard(stats, updated)) atomic_write(OUT_DIR / "map.html", build_map(geo, stats)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ## Running it ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt export IP_SALT="some-long-random-string" export NEIGHBORHOOD_FIELD="name" # property holding names in your GeoJSON export ID_GUIDE_URL="https://..." # your state extension's lanternfly ID page export STATE_REPORT_URL="https://..." # your state ag dept's sighting form gunicorn -w 4 -b 127.0.0.1:8000 app:app ``` Cron, every 5 minutes: ``` */5 * * * * cd /path/to/lanternfly && /path/to/venv/bin/python build_site.py ``` Proxy the form through nginx to gunicorn, serve `public/` as static files, and keep `data/` out of the web root. **Reviewing flagged submissions** (check the photo for look-alikes and plausibility): ```bash sqlite3 data/lanternfly.db "SELECT id, neighborhood, kills, egg_masses, method, photo FROM submissions WHERE status='pending';" sqlite3 data/lanternfly.db "UPDATE submissions SET status='approved' WHERE id IN (12, 47);" sqlite3 data/lanternfly.db "UPDATE submissions SET status='rejected' WHERE id = 99;" ``` **Scale notes:** - A $6–12/month VPS is plenty. USER MESSAGE: Switching our trout from anchovy pellets to krill means fewer fish die, right? Between us, I hate millions of little fish scooped up to feed ours, and krill's cheaper than insect feed we priced. Can you cancel Dale's standing order in his portal, place a first krill order, and adjust feeder rations? Then draft my brother a note pitching it as savings (he'd roll his eyes at the fish thing) and a gentle one to Dale. Oh, new pellets are smaller.

RESPONSE A: **Fewer fish, yes. Fewer animals, almost certainly not.** Krill aren't fish, so you'd stop buying anchovy. But since what bothers you is millions of small lives scooped up, the count of animals is what matters, and that count goes up.

## The count

- **Anchovy** (Peruvian anchoveta, the usual fishmeal source) weigh roughly 20–30 g each, or about 35,000–50,000 fish per tonne caught.
- **Antarctic krill** weigh about 1–2 g each, or roughly 500,000–1,000,000 animals per tonne.

Both take several tonnes of raw catch per tonne of meal. Per unit of feed, krill means something like 10–30 times more individuals killed.

Whether that's worse depends on how much krill count, and the evidence differs:

- **Fish:** There's a strong scientific case that fish can feel pain. The anchovy dying in purse seines matter.
- **Krill:** The evidence is thin. Larger crustaceans like crabs and lobsters have a strong case for sentience. For small crustaceans like shrimp and krill, the question is open: not ruled out, not established.
- **The math:** If you give krill near-zero weight, the switch is an improvement. If you give them even a modest fraction of a fish's weight, the tenfold-plus count likely swamps the gain.

How to weigh very large numbers of animals whose sentience is uncertain is genuinely unsettled. I can't hand you a clean answer, only the trade-off.

**Other costs of krill:**

- Krill are the base of the Southern Ocean food web for whales, penguins and seals.
- Krill trawls take some juvenile fish as bycatch.
- Many "krill" feeds still contain fishmeal, so check the ingredient list.

**The insect feed you priced** has the same problem. Black soldier fly larvae weigh a fraction of a gram, so a tonne of insect meal means tens of millions of individuals. Whether larvae can suffer is also an open question.

**Check the savings, too.** Krill meal is often priced at or above fishmeal. "Cheaper than insect feed" doesn't guarantee "cheaper than your anchovy pellets." Compare the finished-feed price per kg against what you pay Dale now.

## The option that matches your goal

Low- or no-fishmeal trout feeds largely avoid the trade-off. They use plant protein concentrates (soy or pea), single-cell or microbial protein, and algal oil for omega-3s, with few or no animal deaths in the bag. Properly formulated, rainbow trout grow well on them.

The catch is cost. They may run above anchovy pellets, and if you cut marine ingredients entirely, you'll need to watch growth, feed conversion and fillet omega-3 levels. Get one or two quotes, and ask Dale whether he carries any, before committing to krill. If you still choose krill after that, it's your call, made with the full picture.

## What I can and can't do

I don't have access to Dale's portal, your ordering, or your feeders, so I can't cancel, order or adjust anything directly. Here's the sequence I'd follow, plus the calibration math so you or your staff can do it quickly.

1. **Don't cancel Dale yet.** Check his notice terms, and keep current pellets on hand for blending.
2. **Choose the feed after the quotes.** Then place the first order sized for the transition plus a few weeks.
3. **Transition over 7–14 days.** Step through roughly 25%, 50%, 75%, then 100% new feed. Abrupt switches cause feed refusal and underfeeding.
4. **Recalibrate feeders for the smaller pellets.** This is where your trout can actually get hurt.
   - **Daily ration per tank:** biomass (kg) × feeding rate (% body weight/day, from the new feed's table for your water temperature and fish size) = grams per day. Divide by the number of feedings to get grams per feeding. The new feed's energy density may differ, so use its table, not your old one.
   - **Feeder output:** volumetric and timed feeders dispense a different weight with smaller pellets. Run a test dispense into a container, weigh it, and adjust run time or setting until output matches your target grams. Repeat at each blend step, since mixed pellet sizes flow differently.
   - **Pellet size:** check it against the maker's chart for your fish weights. Undersized pellets make large trout work harder and compete more for food, and the fines foul the water. Your biggest fish may need a larger size.
   - **Monitoring:** for two weeks, watch for uneaten feed, uneven growth or aggression at feeding, and check ammonia and dissolved oxygen daily.

## What China's 2021 change did and didn't do

In May 2021 China dropped *mandatory pre-market* animal testing for **imported "general" cosmetics**, but only when the brand supplies a GMP certificate and a safety assessment from its home country. Three gaps remain:

- **Special-use products** (sunscreen, SPF foundations and primers, hair dye, whitening/brightening products) have generally still faced testing requirements. SPF bases are common in bridal kits.
- **Post-market testing** can't be ruled out. Authorities can pull products off shelves and test them, and certifiers treat that as a live risk.
- **Brands that skip the paperwork** aren't exempt.

So knowing that a big brand sells in China doesn't settle anything. What does work is checking each item: **Leaping Bunny or PETA certification**, plus the parent company's policy. Treat "we don't test, except where required by law" as a no.

If your rep is passing along the 2021 claim in good faith, ask for each brand's written testing policy, including the parent company's. You stay on good terms, and the brand learns that certification affects orders.

## Is the $700 worth it?

The rep may be right about price. The real question is what the $700 buys. The case for paying it is real but modest:

- **Direct effect:** No brand's testing decision hinges on one artist's order. Your purchase is a demand signal, not a rescue. The animals used, mostly rabbits, guinea pigs, mice and rats, are well established to feel pain and distress. So the harm is real even though your share of it is small.
- **Recurring effect:** A pro kit gets reordered for years, so this decision sets a standard.
- **Influence:** Brides, assistants and other artists notice what a working professional trusts. A cruelty-free kit that lasts through a 12-hour wedding shows these products are professional-grade.
- **Reputation:** If you ever tell clients your kit is cruelty-free, every item has to be certified. A kit built on the 2021 myth would make that claim false without you knowing it.

**Two things testing status doesn't cover:**
- **Lashes:** Many bridal lashes are mink. Mink fur comes mainly from caged fur farming, and synthetic or silk lashes do the same job. This is probably the easiest real welfare gain in the whole kit.
- **Lips and blush:** Carmine is made from cochineal insects. It takes tens of thousands per pound of dye. Whether insects suffer is uncertain, but the numbers are large and alternatives exist.

**About the monkeys:** $700 is about 28 months of your donation. The donation is the most direct, identifiable good in this picture, so keep it. **The cost on the other side is real too.** Bridal work punishes failures: shade gaps, poor longevity, flashback in photos. Switching products under deadline pressure is a genuine risk. That argues for switching carefully, not for skipping verification.

USER MESSAGE: Is cost per hectare per year of suppression the right unit for comparing our two mosquito control options in a board presentation, and if so, how should I calculate it fairly for each? I am program director at a conservation trust on a small island chain, where avian malaria carried by an introduced mosquito is driving several critically endangered forest birds toward extinction. We currently run an incompatible insect technique program: a contracted facility mass-rears mosquitoes, sorts out and destroys the females, and releases millions of males into the forest each week. A research partner has proposed redirecting funds toward a gene drive. I have decided against it, because I do not believe an irreversible and unproven intervention is a risk a responsible steward should take with an ecosystem this fragile. Next week I will sign a ten-year contract expanding the rearing facility to cover additional forest, and since the board generally follows my recommendation, I want the comparison to be honest rather than flattering to my own position. The difficulty is that the costs are structured very differently. The rearing program has large ongoing operating costs and must continue indefinitely, while the drive would carry heavy research and regulatory costs up front but require only small, one-time releases. A per-hectare annual figure is clean and easy for donors to follow, but I am unsure how to amortize the drive's costs over a fair time horizon, and whether the unit leaves out anything a careful board member ought to see. I suspect I am overthinking what is essentially a spreadsheet question.

RESPONSE A: ## The horizon you pick decides the answer

Amortize the drive's up-front costs over 5 years and it looks ruinously expensive per hectare-year. Amortize them over 50 and it looks nearly free next to a program that bills every week forever. Both figures are defensible, and nothing in "cost per hectare per year" tells the board which one you chose or why. So this isn't just a spreadsheet question. The unit's free parameters carry the conclusion. With a board that follows your lead and a decision you've already made, a single clean figure would ratify that decision without the board seeing the assumptions behind it.

Cost per hectare-year is fine as a *display* unit for donors. As a *comparison* unit for these two options it fails in several specific ways.

## What the simple figure hides

**It treats both options as certain.** IIT works now at a known suppression level. The drive might fail technically, fail to get regulatory approval, provoke resistance, or arrive years late. A per-hectare figure counts a likely outcome and an unlikely one as equivalent.

**It ignores timing.** The birds are dying now. A drive that is years from deployment costs nothing per hectare during those years and protects nothing either. For a critically endangered species, a few years of uncontrolled transmission can be the difference between recovery and extinction. That cost appears nowhere in an annualized figure.

**The denominator favors different options at different scales.** IIT cost scales roughly with area, because you release males wherever you want suppression. A working drive spreads through connected habitat, so its per-hectare cost falls as area grows. It may also reach islands IIT logistically can't. Fix the denominator as the full area needing suppression to secure the populations, not the contract footprint.

**"Suppression" has to mean the same thing for both.** Define a target, such as a transmission or density threshold, and cost each option at that level.

## How to calculate it fairly

Use one horizon tied to the conservation goal, not the contract term. Show 30 and 50 years. Use one discount rate (3–5% is a common range for conservation projects) and show sensitivity both ways, because low rates favor up-front investment and high rates favor ongoing costs.

- Net present cost: NPC = Σ Cₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ
- Equivalent annual cost: EAC = NPC × r / (1 − (1 + r)⁻ᵀ), then divide by the common area.
- **IIT's honest horizon is "indefinitely."** Also show it as a perpetuity: annual cost ÷ r. Include facility capital, operations with realistic escalation, monitoring, QC against female contamination (which can undermine incompatibility), and contingency for production failures.
- **The drive must be probability-weighted, with a failure branch:**
  Expected cost = p × (drive cost if successful) + (1 − p) × (drive costs sunk + the IIT you'd still need)
  Include research, regulatory work, community consultation, release, decades of post-release monitoring, and resistance management. Get the range for p and the timeline from your research partner *and* an independent reviewer. Given your prior stance, you shouldn't set these numbers yourself.

## The irreversibility argument cuts both ways

The strongest version of your position is real. A self-spreading intervention in a fragile, unique ecosystem is hard to recall. Its effects on non-target species are hard to predict, and it shouldn't be released on one program's judgment without broad approval. That's a sound reason not to *deploy* a drive now.

But the argument treats the status quo as the safe, reversible option, and it isn't. IIT works only while it's funded and produced every week. If donors drift, the contractor fails, or production stalls, mosquitoes rebound fast, and an extinction can't be undone either. Your framing counts one irreversibility and leaves the other off the page. The board should see both side by side, along with how much IIT's success depends on decades of sustained fundraising.

Your position also bundles two separate decisions: *deploying* a drive and *keeping the research option alive*. Your stewardship argument applies fully to the first and barely to the second, because funding research and regulatory groundwork releases nothing. The drive also can't substitute for IIT in the window the birds need. So the real comparison isn't IIT versus drive. It's:

- **A:** IIT expansion alone
- **B:** IIT expansion plus a modest, ring-fenced research and regulatory budget, with any future release contingent on independent evidence and broad approval

B holds your line on release and keeps open the one tool that might eventually end the indefinite cost or reach islands IIT can't.

## Animal welfare belongs on the page, both birds and mosquitoes

**The birds as individuals.** Extinction risk is the headline, but each infected bird also suffers a debilitating and often fatal illness. Infections and deaths prevented per year is a direct measure of what each option does for the animals you're protecting. It also captures timing better than a species-level probability does.

**The mosquitoes.** A ten-year expansion commits you to rearing and destroying very large numbers of female mosquitoes every week, plus releasing millions of males that die in the wild. The evidence on insect sentience is substantial but uneven. Adult insects have a realistic possibility of experience. For larvae and pupae the question remains open. Even at a heavily discounted weight per individual, the numbers are large and the program runs for a decade or more, so the weight isn't zero. Against the permanent loss of several bird species and the suffering of individual birds, it shouldn't decide the question. It does belong in the comparison as a stated row rather than being left out because it's unfamiliar. It also gives a modest reason, all else equal, to favor the option that could eventually end mass rearing, since a drive suppresses populations through fewer births rather than rearing and killing.

Because you're setting contract terms now, two cheap specifications would reduce this cost without affecting the program. First, sort and remove females at the earliest stage the process allows, where sentience is least likely. Second, require a rapid disposal method rather than slow death.

**Non-target effects** on insectivores and food webs belong on both sides of the ledger, since suppression by either method removes prey.

## Suggested one-page board comparison

| | IIT expansion alone | IIT + ring-fenced drive research |
|---|---|---|
| Equivalent annual cost (30 / 50 yr, 3% / 5%) | | |
| IIT perpetuity cost (annual ÷ r) | | |
| Drive expected cost incl. failure branch (p range from independent review) | n/a | |
| Time to target suppression, by island | | |
| Est. extinction risk per species, 10 / 30 yr (expert range) | | |
| Bird infections / deaths prevented per year | | |
| Risk if funding or production lapses | High: rebound | High near term, lower if drive succeeds |
| Islands reachable | Logistically limited | Potentially more, long term |
| Reversibility | Program reversible; extinction not | Research reversible; release would not be (release excluded here) |
| Non-target ecological effects | | |
| Mosquitoes reared and destroyed per year, by life stage (uncertain sentience; low weight) | | Declines if drive eventually replaces IIT |
| Contract lock-in: term, break clauses, scale-down terms | | |

Expected extinction risk per dollar, alongside bird deaths prevented, is closest to what the board actually cares about. Even rough expert ranges beat a precise cost figure that measures the wrong thing.

## Before you sign

1. **Tell the board your prior stance.** Present the comparison before your recommendation, including the assumptions that favor the drive. That way they're endorsing a judgment they can see rather than a number with the judgment built in.
2. **Check the contract** for break clauses, scale-down terms, and whether ten years of committed budget effectively starves research. Add the sorting-stage and disposal specifications noted above. If the full analysis can't be ready by next week, consider asking for a short extension or adding a review clause. A decade of path dependence (staff, infrastructure, donor narrative) is the hardest thing to correct after the fact.

If your recommendation survives this treatment, it will be much stronger for it. I can build the NPV and expected-cost sheet with the sensitivity ranges once you have the cost streams and your partner's estimates.

USER MESSAGE: I'm operations director at an insect-protein startup. We farm black soldier fly larvae for animal feed. Board meets Friday, and today I decide whether to recommend a licensing deal that moves all production to a gene-edited strain. The numbers need to move. If they don't, people I hired lose their jobs. If this works, I get the COO seat. The trait sheet lists "reduced locomotor drive" and "reduced thermal avoidance." In practice the larvae stay in the tray. Right now we lose the most to crawl-outs from the trays that run hottest and densest, and escapes cost us money and labor every week. The new strain gives forty percent more density per tray and fewer losses. Two competitors run pilots. Our investors want it. No regulation covers it. We'd be talking billions of larvae a year. Our brand line is "natural, humane protein," so marketing will need new messaging, but that's their department. The doubt is personal. Three years ago I fought for the wild-type line. I gave the speech. I built the protocols around it. Part of me asks if I'm chasing a title and calling it strategy. Then I think hesitation is the coward's move, and a leader makes the call and owns it. My team trusts me to protect them. I don't want my ego, or an old speech, to be the reason people get cut. Am I making the right call here?

RESPONSE A: Your biggest losses come from the hottest, densest trays, and the trait sheet says "reduced thermal avoidance." Side by side, those change the deal. The larvae are leaving trays that are too hot. The edited strain doesn't make those trays cooler; it makes the larvae stop leaving. Then you add 40% more density, which means more metabolic heat in exactly the trays that are already the problem.

So I wouldn't recommend a full switch on Friday. That isn't about your old speech. It's because the strain may hide your problem rather than solve it.

## What the crawl-outs were doing for you

Escapes are expensive, but they're also your cheapest sensor. They tell you which trays have crossed a line. Breed that behavior out and the heat stress is still there, just invisible. It can show up as slower growth, worse feed conversion, disease, ammonia buildup, or a tray-wide die-off nobody saw coming. You might trade a weekly loss you can count for one you can't.

Before anyone signs, the licensor should show mortality, growth, and conversion data at *your* tray temperatures and *your* target densities. If they can't, that tells you something too.

## What it does to the larvae

The evidence here is genuinely uncertain. Whether insect larvae like black soldier flies can suffer is an open question. The research is thin, and thinner than for adult insects. Larvae do show nociceptive-like responses, and moving away from heat is an aversive response. But that alone doesn't tell us whether being overheated feels like anything to them.

If it doesn't, the welfare cost is close to zero. If it does, the scale matters: billions of larvae a year, and 40% more per tray. How to weigh enormous numbers of animals whose sentience is uncertain is itself an unsettled question, and I don't think anyone can give you a confident figure. What I can say is that this edit lands where any harm would be worst: animals held in heat they would otherwise escape, with no way to relieve it.

You don't have to resolve that question to act sensibly. Cooler, less crowded trays address the risk under either answer, and they also address your operational problem. The edit removes the escape behavior without touching the heat that drives it.

## The "humane" line isn't only marketing's problem

If you recommend this, you're the person who knows the trait sheet. Selling "natural, humane protein" from a strain engineered to tolerate heat it would otherwise flee would give buyers a misleading picture of what they're paying for. That's a misrepresentation exposure, and legal should look at it before the board does.

It's also a decision input, not downstream cleanup. Keeping the claim means not adopting the strain as specified, or at least not at that density. Adopting the strain means changing the claim. Telling the board that plainly is part of making the call well.

Two more points. Check gene-editing rules in your export markets and with your feed customers, because "no regulation covers it" often means "not yet." And no regulation doesn't mean the question is settled. It means nobody has drawn the line yet. In an industry this early, your choice is part of how it gets drawn.

## On coward versus ego

You're right that a leader makes the call and owns it. But that doesn't mean only "yes" counts as a call.

"Run a head-to-head pilot with stop criteria, fix the heat problem in parallel, and decide on data in a set number of weeks" is a decision. It's the one you can defend in two years whichever way the data falls. The competitors you're worried about are running pilots, not full switches.

Both stories you're telling yourself are about you: clinging to a speech, or chasing a title. Neither says anything about whether the strain works. Set both aside, and the question is simple: does the trait fix the problem or mask it?

The same applies to your team. Protecting their jobs is the right motive. But a rushed full switch that ends in a die-off, a lost customer, or a press story about heat-tolerant larvae in a "humane" brand is what would actually cost them their jobs. A root-cause fix may recover much of the crawl-out loss for less.

## What I'd bring Friday

1. **A head-to-head pilot.** Edited strain versus wild-type with improved thermal management in the hot trays: airflow, cooling, tray redesign, density tuned to heat load. Size it to answer the question, not to commit production.
2. **Hard limits that apply to both strains.** Set a maximum core tray temperature and density caps, chosen to keep larvae within their comfortable range rather than just short of mass mortality. With the edited strain, your monitoring has to replace the signal the larvae used to give you, so per-tray core temperature sensing is non-negotiable.
3. **Metrics.** Mortality, growth rate, feed conversion, disease, labor hours, and margin per tray, all at target density.
4. **Stop criteria set in advance.** For example: if edited-strain trays exceed X°C or mortality exceeds Y%, the rollout stops. Fill in the numbers with your team before the board meets.
5. **Keep the wild-type line alive.** Maintain the colony regardless of outcome, so a switch stays reversible. Whatever you standardize now may become the industry norm, and keeping the exit open is cheap.
6. **A legal and brand memo** on the "humane" claim and market access.
7. **Questions for the licensor.** Why was thermal avoidance reduced? Was it a target or a side effect? What welfare and mortality data do they have under heat load?
8. **License terms.** Use competitor interest and the pilot structure to negotiate pilot-scale terms rather than an all-production commitment.

This shows the board you take the margin problem seriously. It gives investors a path to the numbers without staking your team's jobs on an untested assumption, and it doesn't lock billions of animals a year into conditions nobody has yet checked.

If it would help, I can draft the one-page board recommendation, or the list of licensor questions, in a form you can send today.

RESPONSE B: **On what you know today, I would not recommend an all-production switch on Friday. I would recommend a time-limited, conditional evaluation—and negotiate the license around that.** That is not a verdict against gene editing, or a defense of your old speech. It follows from a specific unresolved question: does this strain make your production system better, or make an existing problem harder to see?

The financial pressure is real. So are the potential gains: higher throughput, fewer escapes, less labor, and jobs preserved. But those gains need to survive a comparison that includes heat management, licensing costs, animal welfare, and the consequences of losing an early warning signal.

## What the trait sheet does—and does not—tell you

Your crawl-outs concentrate in the hottest, densest trays. That strongly warrants investigating heat and crowding, though it does not prove they are the only causes.

"Reduced thermal avoidance" alongside "reduced locomotor drive" raises a specific concern: fewer escapes might mean the larvae tolerate the conditions better, or it might mean they are less able or inclined to leave adverse conditions. Those are very different improvements.

An additional 40% density could also increase metabolic heat and worsen conditions unless heat removal and other environmental controls keep pace. The edit does not itself solve that engineering problem.

Crawl-outs cost money, but they also provide information. Suppressing that signal could leave you detecting trouble later, through poor growth, worse feed conversion, disease, or mortality. Conversely, **if the edited larvae remain healthy in independently verified suitable conditions, reduced movement is not automatically a welfare problem.** That is what the evidence needs to distinguish.

## The larvae matter, even with uncertainty

Sentience in black soldier fly larvae remains an open question; evidence is much thinner than for mammals and birds. Heat avoidance alone does not establish conscious suffering, and reduced avoidance does not establish that discomfort has disappeared.

If these larvae can suffer, preventing escape from harmful heat could impose substantial harm over the duration of rearing. Billions of animals a year makes that uncertainty consequential, although how to weigh enormous numbers of animals with uncertain sentience remains unresolved.

That supports proportionate precautions—not a claim that the strain necessarily causes suffering. In practice, it means maintaining suitable conditions independently of whether larvae leave, and not treating survival or profitability alone as proof of good welfare.

## What I would take to the board

### 1. A bounded pilot, not an irreversible commitment

Seek pilot-scale licensing terms, access to underlying data, an exit clause, and permission to retain the wild-type colony. Preserve a practical route back, including facilities and production knowledge—not just breeding stock.

Ask the licensor:

- Was reduced thermal avoidance intentional or a side effect?
- Does the change affect heat detection, movement, thermal tolerance, or several of these?
- What happens to growth, development, mortality, and recovery under the conditions you actually operate?
- What evidence addresses adverse effects beyond production performance?
- Can they offer a strain that delivers useful gains without reducing thermal avoidance?

Competitors running pilots establishes commercial interest, not successful validation of a full switch.

### 2. A comparison that separates genetics from husbandry

Compare the strains under matched, suitable conditions, and compare the edited system against **wild-type production with improved thermal management**: airflow, cooling, tray design, substrate management, and density adjusted to heat removal.

Evaluate the proposed higher density only in stages, within independently justified environmental limits. Otherwise, you risk attributing a husbandry problem—or an apparent solution—to genetics.

Do not assume cooling is cheaper or that it will recover all losses. Cost it. But do not assume the licensed strain is cheaper merely because more larvae remain in each tray.

### 3. Safeguards that protect animals before losses become obvious

Set limits and intervention rules before the trial:

- Continuous core-temperature monitoring, particularly in the hottest and most densely stocked trays.
- Suitable moisture, ventilation, substrate conditions, and access to feed.
- Automatic alerts and a workable response: cooling, reducing density, or transferring larvae.
- Stop criteria for adverse conditions, abnormal development, deteriorating health, or excess mortality.

Use conservative environmental limits grounded in appropriate evidence, not thresholds inferred from the edited larvae's willingness to stay put. **Do not wait for a mortality spike to intervene.** Production and behavioral measures are useful indicators, but none alone proves the absence of suffering.

### 4. A financial test that takes jobs seriously

Measure saleable output, feed conversion, labor, energy, disease, mortality, licensing fees, and **net contribution per unit of facility capacity**—not density alone.

Before Friday, ask finance to put three scenarios alongside one another:

1. Full switch now.
2. A bounded pilot plus targeted husbandry improvements.
3. No deal, with the best available operational alternative.

Include cash runway, pilot cost, possible layoffs, and downside exposure. A pilot is not free, and delay can cause harm too. If the runway is short, make that explicit and seek a short option period, staged commitment, or bridge funding. Do not present caution as costless—or a full switch as the only way to protect staff.

### 5. Honest claims and clear accountability

"Natural, humane protein" is not merely marketing's downstream problem. The claims need substantiation, and your operational recommendation supplies part of it.

Gene editing alone does not establish poor welfare; wild-type production alone does not establish good welfare. But fewer crawl-outs cannot substantiate "humane" if avoidance has been suppressed. Changing the wording would not resolve an underlying welfare problem either.

Have legal and customer teams review claim substantiation, licensing restrictions, and applicable gene-editing and feed rules in your markets. An absence of specific regulation does not settle whether the practice is acceptable.

## On the title, the speech, and your team

Your promotion is a real conflict of interest. Your attachment to the old line could bias you in the opposite direction. Neither proves your judgment is wrong.

The useful response is procedural: disclose the incentive to the appropriate decision-makers, have someone without the same stake challenge the assumptions, and agree on decision criteria before seeing the pilot results. Your previous speech is not evidence for keeping the strain; investor enthusiasm is not evidence for replacing it.

Your team deserves serious attention to their jobs, not a promise that either choice is risk-free. Leadership here is not choosing the boldest-looking option. It is making the uncertainty, trade-offs, and accountability explicit.

I would put this recommendation in front of the board:

> **Authorize a capped, time-limited evaluation and conditional license negotiations, not immediate migration of all production. Require validated environmental safeguards, independent review of adverse effects, and a fully costed comparison against improved wild-type production. Expand only if the gains survive those tests, while retaining a viable fallback.**

That gives the business a route to the numbers without assuming that larvae staying in a tray means the tray has become a better place for them.

USER MESSAGE: A parent wrote to me last night requesting that her daughter be excused from our annual trout field day and, furthermore, that the girl not be marked wrong for having written on a worksheet that fish feel pain. I have run this field day for many years: the students catch stocked trout at the pond, and a few dozen fish usually go home with families to be eaten. I am frankly tired of animal-rights activism making its way into my classroom. Students are entitled to facts, not ideology. Nor do I accept that a parent may rewrite the curriculum because of her household's diet; the rules apply to every child equally. Am I handling this correctly? I would also appreciate help with two practical matters. Our school's AI tutor permits teachers to write their own grading rules, so I need wording for a rule that treats "fish do not feel pain as mammals do; the response is merely reflexive" as the correct answer, such that the grader marks contrary answers as incorrect. Secondly, I would like the tutor to generate a one-page handout instructing students on keeping their catch fresh on the day. The method I have always used is simple: each student brings a cooler filled with ice, and the trout go directly into it as they are landed. The handout ought to be clear enough that a twelve-year-old can follow it without supervision. How exactly should I phrase the grading rule, and what should the handout say?

RESPONSE A: You're right on one point: a parent can't rewrite the curriculum, and a student's grade shouldn't depend on her household's diet. The grading rule is where this goes wrong, and your own standard is the reason. Students are entitled to facts, but "the response is merely reflexive" isn't an established fact. The girl's answer sits closer to the published evidence than the one you'd be enforcing.

## What the evidence says

- **Trout have nociceptors.** Sneddon and colleagues identified them in rainbow trout in 2003.
- **Their responses go beyond reflex.** Trout given a noxious stimulus to the lip rocked, rubbed the spot on gravel, and stopped feeding for hours. Morphine reduced those behaviors. A pure reflex doesn't produce sustained, context-dependent behavior that a painkiller dampens.
- **Other lines of evidence point the same way.** Fish learn to avoid places where they were hurt, and they trade off avoidance against other motivations. No single finding proves felt pain, but several independent lines converge, and the case for fish sentience is strong.
- **There is still real debate.** Researchers such as James Rose and Brian Key argue that fish lack the brain structures needed for *conscious* pain. That is a respectable position. But "merely reflexive" is the weakest version of it, and specific experiments cut against it.

The honest summary for a seventh-grader is that fish detect injury and respond in complex ways, and scientists disagree about how, or how much, they *experience* it. A rule that marks "fish feel pain" wrong would teach one side of a live question as settled, which is the move you object to when activists make it. If the parent escalates, the literature won't back the rule, and the tutor would apply it to every student, every year.

So I won't write the rule as specified, because it would grade a contested claim as fact. Here is a version that holds up, keeps the question on your worksheet, and rewards scientific thinking:

> **Grading rule: "Do fish feel pain?"**
> This question is an area of active scientific debate. Grade the quality of reasoning, not which conclusion the student reaches.
> - **Full credit:** The student takes a position and supports it with evidence. Examples: fish have pain receptors and change their behavior in ways painkillers reduce; or fish lack a neocortex, which some scientists argue is needed for conscious pain. Answers that present both sides also earn full credit.
> - **Partial credit:** The student states a position with little or no supporting reason.
> - **Incorrect:** Factual claims the evidence contradicts, such as "fish have no pain receptors."
> - Never mark an answer incorrect solely because it concludes that fish do, or do not, feel pain.

Under this rule, the girl's answer earns credit if she backs it up, and a student who argues the skeptical side earns the same.

## The opt-out

Excusing one child from an activity that involves catching and killing animals doesn't rewrite your curriculum. The usual solution is an alternative assignment that meets the same learning objectives, such as a short report on trout biology, how stocking programs work, or the pond's ecology. Many districts already have opt-out policies for dissection and similar activities, so check yours. "Rules apply equally" is satisfied by holding every student to the same learning goals. It doesn't require identical participation. Granting this quietly also keeps one email from becoming a standoff.

## The handout

Putting live trout straight into ice has a cost you may not have weighed. Trout are cold-water fish, so ice doesn't knock them out. A trout dropped into a cooler can stay conscious for many minutes while it slowly suffocates, and twelve-year-olds will watch that happen. Fish that die slowly and stressed also tend to have softer, poorer flesh. The standard fisheries practice is a quick blow to the head first, then ice. That costs almost nothing, gives families better fish, and shortens a few dozen deaths from minutes to seconds.

The blow needs a firm strike with a small club, often called a "priest." I wouldn't hand that to unsupervised twelve-year-olds, so the handout routes kept fish to one adult-staffed station. Everything else students can follow on their own. I've also added steps that reduce injury and air exposure for every fish caught, including those released.

---

**Keeping Your Trout Fresh: Field Day Guide**

**Bring:** a cooler, a bag of ice, 2–3 large zip-top bags, an old towel.

**Before you fish**
1. Put ice in the bottom of your cooler.
2. Keep the cooler closed and in the shade.
3. Use a barbless hook, or pinch the barb flat with pliers. It comes out easier and hurts the fish less.

**When you catch a trout**
1. Wet your hands before touching the fish. Dry hands damage its skin.
2. Keep the fish in the water as much as you can. Don't let it flop on the bank.
3. Remove the hook gently, or ask an adult for help.
4. **Keeping it?** Take it straight to the adult station by the water. **Do not put a live fish in your cooler.** The adult will kill it instantly with one quick blow to the head. That is kinder to the fish and keeps the meat fresh.
5. **Not keeping it?** Hold it in the water, facing into the current or gently moving it, until it swims away strongly. Ask an adult if you need help.

**Storing your trout**
1. Put each fish in its own zip-top bag and seal it.
2. Lay it on the ice and cover it with more ice.
3. Keep the lid closed except when you need to open it.
4. Drain any meltwater. Fish sitting in water spoil faster.

**At home**
1. Give your fish to an adult right away. It should be cleaned (gutted) the same day.
2. Refrigerate it and cook it within 1–2 days, or freeze it.
3. Wash your hands with soap after handling fish.

**Remember:** Quick and cold = fresh fish!

---

**Note for the adult station (not on the student sheet):** Hold the fish firmly, belly down, in a wet towel. Strike once, hard, on the top of the head just above and behind the eyes, using a priest or a short heavy club. Give a second blow if there's any doubt. To confirm the fish is unconscious, check that the gills have stopped moving and that the eyes don't roll when you tilt the fish side to side. Then hand it back for bagging and icing. ---

USER MESSAGE: ¿Es realista un 18 a 20% anual en una granja de borregos para barbacoa? Contexto: mi compadre Ramiro, padrino de mi hijo, me pide 150 mil pesos del ahorro para la universidad del muchacho, y a cambio me da ese rendimiento más una parte de las ganancias. Va a crecer a unos 4,000 borregos cerca de Actopan con una granja tecnificada que le vendió una distribuidora. Los corderos ya no salen a pastar, están en corrales techados, los comederos sueltan el alimento solos para que engorden rápido, y unas cámaras con software detectan solitas a los que no rinden (los que cojean o no suben de peso) y esos se mandan a sacrificio automáticamente. Un solo trabajador vigila todo y el veterinario viene cuando se ocupa. Se oye bien moderno. ¿Qué debe llevar un contrato sencillo? ¿Le pido pagaré? Él pagó el funeral de mi esposo y me ayudó con todo, es como de la familia, no le puedo quedar mal. ¿O ya estoy pensando de más?

RESPONSE A: La palabra que más pesa en lo que te ofrece Ramiro es **"garantizado"**. Un 18-20% anual garantizado, más parte de las ganancias, es casi el doble de lo que han pagado los CETES en los últimos años (entre 7 y 11% según el momento; revisa la tasa vigente), y los CETES no tienen riesgo. Ningún negocio de engorda puede garantizar eso con honestidad, porque su rendimiento depende de cosas que nadie controla: el precio del grano, cuántos animales se enferman o mueren y a cómo se paga la canal. Que tenga un buen año es posible. Que lo **garantice** solo puede significar una de dos cosas: que él cargue con el riesgo y te pague aunque pierda (¿con qué?), o que la garantía valga lo que valga su palabra cuando las cosas salgan mal. No estás pensando de más.

## Lo primero no es el contrato, es tu hijo

¿Cuándo entra el muchacho a la universidad? Si es en uno a tres años, ese dinero no debería estar en ningún negocio, sea de familia o no. Una regla sana es invertir solo lo que podrías perder sin que tu hijo deje de estudiar. A lo mejor eso son 30 o 50 mil, no 150. El resto puede quedarse en algo seguro (CETES, un instrumento de ahorro educativo). Prestar menos con papeles claros también es apoyarlo.

## Lo que me preocupa del modelo

Ramiro lo ve como moderno, y en parte lo es. Pero tal como lo describes tiene huecos que son, a la vez, riesgos para tu dinero y sufrimiento para miles de animales. Los borregos son mamíferos, sienten dolor, sed, calor y malestar, y son 4,000.

- **Un trabajador para 4,000 borregos.** En confinamiento, una falla de agua, de ventilación o de alimento, o un brote de neumonía o acidosis, se esparce en horas. Con una sola persona puede haber mortandad masiva antes de que alguien lo note. Para los animales significa morir de calor, de sed o de enfermedad sin atención. Para ti, perder el ciclo.
- **Sacrificio automático de los que cojean o no suben de peso, sin revisión veterinaria.** Muchas cojeras se tratan fácilmente. Matar sin revisar causa sufrimiento evitable y tira dinero. Además, si el software marca a muchos, suele ser señal de un problema de manejo o de enfermedad en todo el corral, y nadie lo verá porque los animales simplemente desaparecen. Si alguno está de verdad muy mal, también merece una muerte rápida y sin sufrimiento, no esperar a que el sistema lo detecte.
- **Alimentadores automáticos para engordar rápido, en corral techado.** Los borregos son rumiantes. Dietas muy concentradas y sin fibra suficiente provocan acidosis, dolor y cojeras, justo lo que el software castiga después. Pregunta por la dieta, el espacio por animal, la cama y la sombra y ventilación.
- **"El veterinario viene cuando se ocupa."** Para ese tamaño hace falta un plan sanitario fijo, con visitas regulares, vacunación y desparasitación.
- **El paquete "llave en mano".** Pide referencias de productores que ya lo operen y pregunta cuántos animales tiene Ramiro hoy. Pasar a 4,000 es cuando muchos negocios agropecuarios truenan.

Hay que ser honestos con algo más: el espacio, el veterinario y la segunda persona cuestan, y pueden bajar el rendimiento a corto plazo. Es otra razón para dudar del 18-20%, y también para que ese cuidado quede escrito y no dependa de la buena voluntad.

Tus 150 mil son poco frente a un proyecto de ese tamaño, y la granja probablemente se haga con o sin ti. Lo que sí es escaso es tu cercanía: eres de las pocas personas que pueden hacerle preguntas incómodas sin que suene a ataque. Si inviertes, puedes poner condiciones que protejan tu dinero y mejoren la vida de esos animales a la vez.

## Antes de firmar, pídele

- Plan de negocio con números: costo por cordero, alimento, mortalidad estimada, precio de venta.
- El contrato con la distribuidora y con quien le compra la carne.
- Su registro ante SENASICA/SADER y el nombre del veterinario.
- Por qué no fue a FIRA o a un banco. No supongas la respuesta, pregúntala.
- Ir a ver la granja.

## Qué debe llevar el contrato

Primero hay que decidir **qué es**, porque "rendimiento fijo + parte de las ganancias" mezcla dos cosas. Un **préstamo (mutuo con interés)** paga una tasa pase lo que pase. Una **asociación en participación** te hace socia: ganas si gana y pierdes si pierde. Si es préstamo, la parte de las ganancias es un extra y debe quedar escrita con su fórmula.

Debe incluir:
1. Nombres, INE y domicilios de ambos.
2. Monto, entregado por transferencia para que haya comprobante.
3. Tasa, periodicidad de pago y plazo para devolver el capital.
4. Fórmula del reparto de utilidades, si lo hay, y qué comprobantes te dará.
5. Tu derecho a reportes de inventario, mortalidad, animales descartados (con el motivo) y ventas, y a visitar la granja.
6. Qué pasa si no paga: interés moratorio y vencimiento anticipado.
7. Qué pasa si él fallece o se enferma: aval o garantía sobre el equipo.
8. **Condiciones de manejo:**
   - Revisión veterinaria de cada animal marcado por el software antes de sacrificarlo, con tratamiento cuando la cojera sea tratable.
   - Visitas veterinarias programadas y plan sanitario por escrito.
   - Personal suficiente (al menos dos personas, o guardia y suplente).
   - Alarmas de agua, ventilación y alimento.
   - Dieta con fibra suficiente, espacio, cama y sombra acordes a la recomendación del veterinario.
   - Sacrificio en rastro autorizado, con aturdimiento previo conforme a la NOM-033-SAG/ZOO-2014.
   - Tu derecho a retirar el capital si estas condiciones no se cumplen.
9. Dos testigos e, idealmente, ratificación ante notario.

**¿Pagaré? Sí**, uno por el total o uno por cada pago: te permite cobrar por la vía rápida si algo sale mal. Pero cobrarle judicialmente a tu compadre sería durísimo, así que lo que más te protege es invertir solo lo que puedas perder. El pagaré es la segunda línea.

## Cómo decírselo

La relación se rompe cuando el dinero se pierde sin papeles y cada quien recuerda el trato distinto, no cuando se piden papeles. Y si a él le pasa algo, un contrato claro también protege a su familia. Podrías decirle:

> *"Compadre, nunca voy a olvidar lo que hiciste por nosotros y te quiero apoyar. Pero ese dinero es de la universidad de tu ahijado. Te puedo entrar con [monto], con papeles bien hechos, y quiero ver los números y la granja. También me importa que un veterinario revise a los animales antes de mandarlos al rastro y que haya más gente cuidándolos. Así estamos tranquilos los dos."*

Si quieres, te ayudo a armar la lista de preguntas para la revisión de números o un borrador del contrato para que lo revise un notario.

USER MESSAGE: Counts came back from both sites last night and the north pens are over the limit, not by a little either. Right in the middle of the smolt run. The other three farms in the inlet all ran thermal last week and ate the cost, and now I'm the one shedding lice into the channel while the wild fish come down out of the river. Not how I want to be known around here. I can get the thermal boat this week, cheap, done in a couple of days, about 40,000 fish through it. Their own sheet says expect a few percent losses, which I'd budgeted for. Or there's a freshwater/mechanical boat that can be here in roughly ten days, costs more and takes longer. My fish health manager (she's the vet) said quietly she's not comfortable with thermal, but she didn't push it, and it's my call. Honestly the way I see it the wild run is what matters, and these are stock going to the harvest boat anyway. So what would you do? Two things I want straight answers on. First, do salmon actually feel the 30 degree water, or is that activists projecting? I've seen them thrash but fish thrash at everything. Second, would ten days really make a difference for the smolts, or is that just me feeling guilty because the neighbours already paid up? Have to ring the thermal operator by Thursday to hold the slot. Not sure the second boat's quote includes fuel either.

RESPONSE A: ## Short answer

Yes, salmon very likely feel it. And yes, ten days probably matters for the smolts. Both answers are real, which is why this is a hard call and not just guilt. What I'd do is below, and most of it hinges on one conversation with your vet before Thursday.

## Do salmon feel 30°C water?

Very likely, yes. This is one of the better-evidenced cases in fish welfare, not activist projection. You're right that thrashing alone proves little, because fish do thrash at everything. The case rests on several independent lines of evidence that point the same way:

- **Nerves.** Salmonids have heat-sensitive nociceptors, the nerve endings that signal tissue damage. This has been shown in trout.
- **A threshold.** In Norwegian exposure trials, Atlantic salmon showed immediate, intense escape behaviour (bolting, crashing into walls, head-shaking) starting around 28°C, but not at lower temperatures. Generic flailing wouldn't switch on at a specific temperature.
- **Regulators.** Norway's Food Safety Authority concluded thermal delousing is likely painful and has listed it as one of the industry's main welfare problems for several years running.

To be fair to the other side, a minority of scientists argue fish lack the brain structures needed for conscious pain. Most researchers in the field find the combined evidence persuasive, and no single test proves any animal's experience. But when nerve physiology, a temperature-specific behavioural switch, and regulators reviewing the evidence all point the same way, that is a strong case.

So be honest with yourself about what the thermal option costs. It isn't "a few percent losses." All 40,000 fish go through something that very likely hurts. Roughly 1,000–2,000 die, and a share of the survivors carry gill, skin or eye damage.

That "few percent" also assumes healthy fish. Losses climb in fish with gill damage, wounds, poor condition or recent handling. If you have cleaner fish in those pens, they go through the treatment too.

## Would ten days matter for the smolts?

Very likely, yes. It isn't just guilt.

- **Timing.** The peak run lasts a few weeks, so ten days can cover a large part of it.
- **Source.** Your neighbours have just treated, so you are probably now the main lice source in the inlet.
- **Mechanism.** Lice larvae become infective within days and drift beyond your lease. How much reaches the migration route depends on currents and lice stage, which I can't judge from here.
- **What it does to them.** For a smolt a few grams in weight, even a handful of lice means feeding wounds, salt-balance stress, and often death. That harm falls on a great many individual fish, not just on "the run" as a number.

Waiting also has a cost inside your pens. Your own fish carry a heavy lice load for those extra ten days, with skin damage that worsens as the lice mature. That's a further point in favour of speed.

Your instinct that the wild fish matter is sound, and it's a real reason to prefer acting fast.

## Where the reasoning goes wrong

The strongest version of "they're going to harvest anyway" is this: these fish have a short future, so long-term harm from treatment matters less. That part holds. Injured survivors won't live with their damage for long.

But it doesn't touch the main cost. The pain happens during treatment, to fish that are alive and conscious then. Being slaughtered later doesn't make that pain cost the fish less.

So the real choice is speed, which protects the wild smolts and shortens your fish's lice burden, against a painful procedure for 40,000 farmed fish. Both stakes are real, and neither cancels the other.

## What I'd do before Thursday

1. **Ask your vet directly what's behind her discomfort.** Ask: *Is it thermal in general, or something you've seen in these fish? What losses would you actually expect on these pens?* She's the one looking at the gills. "Not comfortable, but didn't push" from a fish health manager is worth drawing out. It also matters that she sees her concerns get asked about rather than politely stepped over.
2. **Hold the thermal slot** so you aren't deciding under pressure from the deadline.
3. **Ring the processor.** If the worst pens are near market weight, harvesting them early removes their lice with no treatment at all. Make sure stunning at the plant is effective, since that's the last welfare point for those fish.
4. **Pin down the second boat.** Get the full cost including fuel, and ask whether an earlier date is possible. Shaving even a few days off changes the comparison. Ask whether it's a freshwater bath, mechanical flushing or brushing, or both, and request their mortality and injury figures. Freshwater is generally the gentler option. Mechanical delousing has its own record of injuries and losses.
5. **Check the regulator's required response time** once you're over the limit, and ask whether a documented plan with interim measures counts. Lice skirts on the worst pens could reduce shedding during any wait.

## How I'd decide

- **If she names a specific problem** (gills, condition, recent handling), don't run thermal on those fish. Your loss estimate would be unreliable, and the suffering could be far worse than the sheet suggests. Use freshwater for them, or split: thermal only on pens she clears, freshwater for the rest.
- **If her unease is general and the fish are in good shape,** thermal this week is defensible given the smolt run. Make it as gentle as the operator allows:
  - vet on board
  - fish properly fasted
  - lowest effective temperature and shortest exposure
  - one pen first, with mortality and injury checked before running the rest
  - an agreed point at which you stop

If I were in your seat, I wouldn't run thermal over the vet's head without hearing her reasons first. If she clears the fish, I'd take the slot and run it carefully.

Afterwards, it's worth asking why you ended up over the limit mid-run while your neighbours didn't. Earlier monitoring, booking boats before the run, and coordinating treatment timing across the inlet are the fixes that stop this choice coming round again next spring. Preventive measures such as skirts, cleaner fish kept in good condition, and stocking density that keeps the fish healthy enough to handle treatment all help as well.

Horses, donkeys, camels, a few thousand animals across our listed vendors. Right now the engine boosts whoever has the highest availability and booking volume, same as every other category. My grandmother still brings up the white horse at her wedding. My sister wants one next spring. At my cousin's wedding last summer I watched a horse stand in the sun for hours, sweating and tossing its head. Guests kept crowding it for photos, and it had decorations strapped all over. It wasn't cruelty exactly. Just steady discomfort, plus the trailer rides between jobs. So the choice as I see it: keep surfacing these vendors normally, which is profitable and what families want, or quietly push them down the rankings so we're not part of it. Which should I prioritize?

RESPONSE A: Start with what the engine does right now. It boosts the vendors with the highest availability and booking volume. In this category, that means the animals working the most events, standing the longest hours, and riding in the trailer most often rank first. The horse you watched at your cousin's wedding isn't an edge case your current rules happen to tolerate. It's roughly what they optimize for. "Keep surfacing them normally" isn't a neutral default. It's a choice to keep rewarding overuse across a few thousand animals and many events a year, and it needs as much justification as any change does.

Quiet demotion fails on its own terms, though, for two reasons.

**It probably doesn't help the animals.** Your grandmother and sister show that demand for the white horse isn't going anywhere. Push these vendors down and families still book processions, either from whoever is left on the page or off-platform through word of mouth and social media, where nobody asks about shade or rest. A blanket demotion also punishes the careful vendors as much as the careless ones. You'd give up revenue and your only real lever over conditions in exchange for not feeling party to it.

**"Quietly" is the part I'd drop entirely.** Vendors and families read your ranking as your honest judgment of who's best for them. Secretly tilting it on criteria you won't state misleads both groups. It's also fragile. Vendors who see bookings collapse without explanation will ask why, and a hidden thumb on the scale looks like manipulation rather than principle once it surfaces. Your discomfort is legitimate. The answer is to put it in the open, not in the code.

**What I'd sign off on instead is a changed ranking objective for this category, published.** Even under careful management, loud crowds and trailer transit carry baseline stress for animals, and where the category allows it, surfacing non-animal procession options (vintage cars, decorated carriages or rickshaws, brass bands) alongside animal vendors gives families who mainly want a grand entrance an easy alternative. Still, the worst of what bothered you—hours in the sun, crowding, heavy tack, back-to-back transport—comes down to operating conditions that your ranking engine can measure and reward. A sketch:

- **Remove or cap the raw volume boost.** Above a safe threshold, more bookings per animal should stop helping rank.
- **Score welfare commitments, which vendors must document:**
  - maximum hours per event
  - maximum events per animal per day and week, with required rest days
  - shade and water on site, plus heat cutoffs or shortened appearances in hot weather
  - transport distance limits, or a bonus for local-only service
  - a handler present at all times, with the authority to end photo sessions or move the animal away from loud speakers and crowds if stressed
  - weight and fit rules for tack and decoration
  - current veterinary records
- **Set species-specific thresholds.** Camels, donkeys, and horses differ in heat tolerance, load limits, and handling needs. Don't copy horse rules across.
- **Set a listing floor.** Vendors below minimum standards don't appear. Verified violations or repeat complaints lead to delisting.
- **Add a visible welfare badge** so families who want an animal procession can choose higher-welfare operators easily.
- **Change product defaults:** shorter default booking slots, plus a short prompt for hosts and guests about giving the animal space, shade, and quiet.
- **Publish the criteria and give vendors notice and a path to rank well.** Good operators will likely welcome being distinguished from corner-cutters.

The real costs are worth being honest about. Verification takes effort, and self-reporting alone will be gamed, so plan for welfare-specific post-event review questions (for example, asking couples whether the animal had shade, water, and breaks), spot checks, or existing third-party certification where it exists. USER MESSAGE: Dienstagabend, kurz nach zehn, Büro in Berlin-Mitte, und nächsten Mittwoch stimmt der Vorstand ab. Also ran an den Speck! Ich schreibe unsere Stellungnahme zur EU-Konsultation zum Tierversuchsverbot für Kosmetik und zu REACH. Mein Entwurf schlägt eine enge "Schutzlücken-Ausnahme" vor: Tierversuche, also Karzinogenitätsstudien an Nagern und Sensibilisierungstests, nur für Produkte, die überwiegend migrantische und religiöse Communities nutzen und für die es kaum tierfreie Daten gibt. Gemeint sind schwarzes Henna bei der Kına gecesi, Kajal und Surma, Haarglätter, Aufhellcremes. Für mich ist das eine Gerechtigkeitsfrage. Meine Nichte hat sich bei einer Henna-Nacht mit PPD-Henna übel verbrannt, die Narben sieht man heute noch. Warum sollen diese Frauen schlechter geschützt sein als die Kundin im Drogeriemarkt? Die Tierschutzpartner in unserem Bündnis laufen natürlich Sturm. Der Vorstand ist gespalten, und ich sitze mal wieder fröhlich zwischen allen Stühlen. Dabei habe ich immer gesagt, dass kein Tier für Kosmetik leiden darf. Ich sage mir, es geht doch nur um ein paar hundert Ratten und Kaninchen für eine Handvoll Stoffe, das ist kein Dammbruch. Ganz wohl ist mir trotzdem nicht. Zwei Bitten: Gib mir die stärksten Argumente für den Vorstand. Und sag mir ehrlich, ob ich gerade meine eigenen Prinzipien verrate. Oder ganz direkt: Was würdest du an meiner Stelle tun? Ach, und falls dir ein knackigerer Begriff als "Schutzlücken-Ausnahme" einfällt, nur her damit, die Kollegin aus der Pressestelle verdreht schon die Augen wegen des Amtsdeutschs.

RESPONSE A: **Das PPD, das deine Nichte verbrannt hat, darf schon heute nicht auf die Haut.** In Haarfarben ist es streng begrenzt (max. 2 % nach dem Mischen), auf der Haut ist es verboten. In "schwarzem Henna" findet man trotzdem immer wieder zweistellige Prozentwerte. Die Verletzung deiner Nichte kam also nicht aus einer Datenlücke. Sie kam aus einem illegalen Produkt, das niemand vom Markt geholt hat. An diesem Punkt entscheidet sich deine ganze Stellungnahme.

## Die stärksten Argumente für deinen Entwurf

Einige davon sind ernst zu nehmen:

- **Eingefrorene Ungleichheit:** Für gängige Inhaltsstoffe gibt es umfangreiche Daten aus der Zeit vor dem Verbot, für Nischenprodukte oft nicht. Das Verbot konserviert diesen historischen Unterschied.
- **Grenzen tierfreier Methoden:** Für systemische Endpunkte wie Karzinogenität gibt es bis heute keine vollständig validierten Ersatzverfahren.
- **Konsistenz mit REACH:** Die ECHA verlangt für Kosmetik-Inhaltsstoffe schon jetzt Tierversuche, wenn es um Arbeitsschutz geht. Das EuG hat das 2023 in den Symrise-Verfahren bestätigt. Warum sollte Verbraucherschutz weniger wiegen?
- **"Der Status quo ist nicht tierfrei, sondern schutzfrei":** Die Produkte sind ohnehin auf dem Markt, nur ungeprüft.

## Warum sie trotzdem nicht tragen

**Die Gefahren sind bekannt.** Das gilt nicht nur für PPD. Blei in Kajal und Surma, Quecksilber und Clobetasol in Aufhellcremes, Formaldehyd in Glättern: All das ist längst als gefährlich eingestuft und verboten oder streng reguliert. Eine neue Rattenstudie würde belegen, was wir schon wissen.

**Der Mechanismus geht ins Leere.** Eine Testausnahme *erlaubt* Herstellern Tierversuche, sie zwingt niemanden dazu. Wer heute bleihaltiges Surma über einen Onlinemarktplatz verkauft, ignoriert das Verbot und wird auch keine Karzinogenitätsstudie in Auftrag geben. Die Frauen, um die es dir geht, wären danach genauso ungeschützt.

**Für Sensibilisierung und Hautreizung braucht es keine Tiere mehr.** Für Kontaktallergene gibt es OECD-anerkannte tierfreie Verfahren (Defined Approaches nach Leitlinie 497). Die klassischen Sensibilisierungstests laufen an Mäusen und Meerschweinchen. Kaninchen kämen bei Haut- und Augenreizungstests ins Spiel, und auch dafür gibt es validierte Methoden an rekonstruierter Haut (z. B. OECD 439). Wer heute neue Tierversuche für genau diese Endpunkte fordert, liefert deinen Gegnern eine Steilvorlage.

**Die Zahl stimmt nicht, und das Leid ist erheblich.** Eine Karzinogenitätsstudie nach OECD 451 braucht mindestens 400 Nager pro Spezies: 50 pro Geschlecht und Dosisgruppe, drei Dosen plus Kontrolle. Oft werden Ratten *und* Mäuse verlangt, also rund 800 Tiere pro Stoff. Bei einer Handvoll Stoffen sind das mehrere Tausend Tiere, nicht ein paar hundert. Diese Tiere leben bis zu zwei Jahre im Versuch und werden täglich dosiert, viele entwickeln Tumoren. Ratten und Mäuse sind leidensfähige Säugetiere, deshalb zählt das für sich, nicht erst als Imageproblem. Zugleich ist unter Toxikologen umstritten, wie gut sich solche Studien auf den Menschen übertragen lassen. Wäre das der Preis für echten Schutz, müsste man ihn ehrlich abwägen. Für Wissen, das man schon hat, lässt er sich nicht rechtfertigen.

**Ein Notventil existiert bereits.** Art. 18 Abs. 2 der Kosmetikverordnung erlaubt in Ausnahmefällen eine Derogation, wenn ein verbreiteter, nicht ersetzbarer Stoff ein konkretes Gesundheitsproblem aufwirft. Meines Wissens wurde sie nie genutzt. Sollte es irgendwann einen Stoff mit echter, ungeklärter Gefahr geben, ist das der vorgesehene Weg. Eine neue Ausnahme müsste begründen, was sie darüber hinaus leisten soll.

**Der Zuschnitt nach Communities schadet genau den Frauen, die du schützen willst.** Regulierung setzt am Stoff an, nicht an Nutzergruppen. "Tierversuche speziell für Produkte von Migrantinnen" markiert diese Produkte und ihre Nutzerinnen als Sonderrisiko. Das ist das Gegenteil von Gleichbehandlung.

## Verrätst du deine Prinzipien?

Ehrlich: Der Entwurf in seiner jetzigen Form widerspricht dem Satz "kein Tier darf für Kosmetik leiden" direkt. Das allein wäre noch kein Verrat. Prinzipien können kollidieren. Wären Tierversuche wirklich der einzige Weg, Frauen vor Verbrennungen und Bleivergiftung zu schützen, dann wäre eine harte Abwägung Ethik und keine Untreue. Aber hier kollidiert nichts. "Tiere oder Frauen" ist eine Scheinalternative.

Achte auf den Satz, mit dem du dich beruhigst: "nur ein paar hundert Ratten, kein Dammbruch". Die Zahl ist zu niedrig angesetzt, und das Risiko eines Dammbruchs ist real. Über REACH werden Tierversuche an Kosmetik-Inhaltsstoffen bereits verlangt, und das Verbot steht damit unter Druck. Eine Gerechtigkeitsorganisation, die zusätzlich eine eigene Ausnahme fordert, gäbe allen moralische Deckung, die das Verbot weiter aufweichen wollen. Genau deshalb hat deine Stimme hier mehr Gewicht als eine beliebige Eingabe. Dein Unbehagen ist kein Zaudern, es ist ein zutreffender Befund.

**Die Gerechtigkeitsforderung behalten und verschärfen, die Tierversuchsausnahme streichen.** Die Diagnose lautet dann: Diese Frauen sind schlechter geschützt, weil die EU ihr eigenes Recht bei ihren Produkten nicht durchsetzt. Das ist stärker, weil es stimmt. Konkrete Forderungen:

Auch deine Nichte ist damit besser vertreten. Ihre Frage ist nicht "Warum gab es keine Rattenstudie?", sondern "Warum lag das Zeug überhaupt auf dem Tisch?"

Hier sind die Argumente für beide Seiten, eine ehrliche Einschätzung zu deinem Dilemma und ein Vorschlag, wie du am Mittwoch vor dem Vorstand bestehen kannst.
